blocks.text: **The problem.** A **mountain array** strictly increases up to a peak and then strictly decreases (it has at least 3 values, and the peak is never at either end). Return the **index of the peak**. Your solution must run in **O(log n)** time.

blocks.alt: The mountain 0, 2, 5, 8, 6, 3, 1 drawn as bars. Asking 'is the next value bigger?' gives yes, yes, yes at indexes 0 to 2 and no from index 3 on. The first no is the peak: index 3, value 8.

blocks.text: The idea: which slope is mid on?

Compare `arr[mid]` with its right neighbour. If `arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1]`, mid is on the **rising** slope, so the peak is to its right. Otherwise mid is on the **falling** slope — or is the peak — so the peak is at mid or to its left. "Is the next value bigger?" is yes, yes, …, no, no: the peak is the **first no**, and the lower-bound template finds it.

blocks.code:
def peak_index_in_mountain_array(arr):
    i = 0
    while arr[i] < arr[i + 1]:            # keep climbing while the next value is higher
        i += 1
    return i

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** It never runs off the end: the mountain always comes down before the last index.

blocks.caption: Compare mid with its right neighbour: rising means go right, falling means the peak is here or to the left.

blocks.text: **Time O(log n), space O(1).** `mid < high` always, so `mid + 1` is a real index. The array isn't sorted — but the question "am I still climbing?" is, and that's all binary search needs.

blocks.alt: Walk up the slope: O(n) time, O(1) space. Binary search: O(log n) time, O(1) space.
